blocks.text: Three radar stations logged it within the same eleven minutes: a mass entering atmosphere on a decel curve no debris follows and no aircraft survives. By the time the analysts at three separate agencies had stopped arguing about whose desk it belonged on, it was down — somewhere in an eight-mile radius of national forest in the Olympic wilderness, and gone from every scope that had been watching it.

Within six hours there were trucks at the tree line and a no-fly order over half a county, and a very quiet, very old fear moving through rooms with no windows: not *what is it*, but *what does it want, and how fast can we get there first.*
They had eight miles of forest to search. They did not know yet that they were looking for a hill.
Walt found the creek before he found anything else — water over stone, a small, ordinary music — and it was there, kneeling to drink, that he saw the shape half-fallen into a bank of stinging nettle.

Grey-green skin going ash at the fingers. A throat with two ridges where a throat should have one. And already, even as he watched, small dark filaments unspooling from a band at its wrist and going still again, like something that had tried to move and given up.

The alien did not wake. Somewhere past midnight its breathing went from labored to shallow to nothing, and Walt sat with the body in a silence too complete for any forest he'd walked through in three weeks of walking.
The band did not wait for permission. It came loose from a dead wrist and began, unhurried, to cross the two feet of dirt between one body and the next.

Up close it was not metal. Metal was the wrong thought entirely — Walt only had that word ready because no other word fit better. It was matte and faintly damp-looking, the color of a healed bruise, and it moved the way slow things move when they very badly do not want to be cold.

He understood, with a clarity he wouldn't be able to explain later even to himself, that it wasn't reaching for his wrist so much as it was *reaching for his warmth* — the way a hand reaches toward a fire, indifferent to whose fire it is.

The first touch was not painful. It was intimate in a way that made his skin want to be somewhere else. A pressure, then a give, then the unmistakable, wrong sensation of something finding a seam in him he hadn't known was a seam — the thin skin over the radial pulse — and going *in*, not around.

He did not scream. He made a sound that had no ancestry in language at all, and then it was under his skin, and the pain arrived a full two seconds behind the fact of it, the way thunder arrives behind lightning: the body always the last to be informed.
For an hour he could feel it *deciding things.*

Not thoughts — nothing so orderly. More like weather moving through a house, testing which doors were unlocked. He felt a coldness spread up the inside of his forearm and understood, distantly, that whatever it was, it was not warming *itself* so much as *building* the means to stay warm — laying down some thread of itself alongside the vein, patient, the way ivy is patient with a wall.

He vomited twice. His vision, for about four minutes, doubled and would not uncross. And then, all at once, it stopped being an invasion and became something closer to a held breath let out. The thing under his skin went quiet the way something goes quiet once it has found what it needed.
When he looked, there was no wound. There was only a faint marbling under the skin at his wrist, like a bruise seen through water, already fading toward invisible.
The days after were not dramatic so much as *wrong* in ways too small to report to anyone, had there been anyone to report them to.

He needed less food and did not miss it. His hearing sharpened past what should have been possible for a man his age — he could parse individual voices from a search team two ridgelines away, though he had no context yet for why there would be a search team at all. Colors arrived a half-second before he consciously registered seeing them, so that for the first several days the world had the quality of a film very slightly out of sync with its own sound.

Worse, and more private: something in him now flinched from cold the way it never had before — not fear, precisely, but an animal aversion, as if some new tenant in his body had opinions about the thermostat and no patience for being ignored.

He did not think of it as a passenger, not yet. He thought of it, when he let himself think of it at all, as *weather that had chosen to live inside his weather* — and he had no idea, none at all, whether it intended to stay a guest.
The pull came on the fourth day, northwest, toward a meadow where the grass grew too even and the birds kept a rough, unbroken silence forty yards wide.

He went because the thing in his blood wanted him to, and because he had nothing left in his own life pulling him anywhere else. What he found there was not a ship in the shape ships are supposed to have. It was a hill that breathed — so slowly the movement was only visible if you watched the same tuft of grass for the length of a held breath, rising, and rising, and then, unbearably, letting go.

It had not landed so much as it had *settled*, the way something enormous settles into sleep. And somewhere behind him, though he didn't know it yet, three separate trucks were closing the same eight-mile radius from three separate directions, following instruments that had no idea they were tracking something that had already decided, long before any of them arrived, exactly who it had come to keep.
